## Introduction

Students are learning to work with Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems more and more [@kumarGuidingStudentsUsing2024] as AI is playing a bigger part in student's academic work, school projects and school policy. Is this affecting their freedom to act?

The freedom to act according to one's own intention and volition is often described as **agency** [@skinnerGuideConstructsControl]. It is this freedom that is described as _achieved agency_ when it is **realised** "through the active engagement of individuals with aspects of their contexts-for-action" [@biestaAgencyLearningLifecourse2007], that always exists in an temporal-relational _ecology_ [@biestaHowAgencyPossible]. This _achieved agency_ is under pressure when systems circulate responsibility among human and non-human actors[@leonardiHomoAgenticusAge2025].

The distinction between human and technological agency blurs with Agentic AI (AAI), as AAI can operate (semi-)autonomously and pursue complex goals with little human intervention [@acharyaAgentic2025]. AAI uses instances of Generative AI (GenAI) interfacing with eachother creating seemingly autonomous and agentic systems, as a next step from the GenAI chat-platforms widely in use among students already [@silvennoinenStudentsUsageGenAI2025].

The _iterational_ aspect of @emirbayerWhatAgency1998's agency upon which @biestaAgencyLearningLifecourse2007 based the _achieved agency_ is exposed in structure and collective beliefs, as _truth_ expressed in instruments such as policies or punitive action [@Foucault1980TruthPower p.131], or as expressed by teachers in their narratives or dispositions [@nesporRoleBeliefsPractice1987]. Beliefs about "inevitability of technology" and the cult of innovation [@winnerCultInnovationIts2018] pervade, while at the same time mistrust and weariness tries to keeps AI out of universities [@guestUncriticalAdoptionAI2025]. Technology is never just neutral nor is it inherently good or bad [@morrowWhenTechnologiesMakes2014; @heyndelsTechnologyNeutrality2023] it is there to be assistive to our human needs [@arora2024pessimism p. 32], and changes us just as much as we change it [@bruno1994technical, p.33].

Students navigate these punitive faculties, policies and teacher narratives as ecology in which they need to realize goals, their agency changing from situation to situation. Is Agentic AI infringing on their intentional volitions realized as _achieved agency_ as the temporal-relational _ecology_ changes?

## Knowledge Gap

Literature focusing on AAI is scarce, unlike the literature for GenAI, which is closely related as precursor to AAI. This shows the need to further examine the phenomenon of AAI in relation to students. Where GenAI is used in studies results can be used as corollary for the type of results for AAI.

The way AAI or GenAI is influencing agency in students seems not to have been studied, apart from the influence it has on critical thinking [@surianoStudentInteractionChatGPT2025], and why and how they use it for studying [@silvennoinenStudentsUsageGenAI2025].

While research has been done about future projections of human agency in conjunction with AI in decision making [@pewFutureHuman2023] and in education [@moutaWhereAgencyMoving2025] it does not deal with how achieved agency for humans now. Or how AAI is changing realized intentions.

Theorizations of agency by @biestaAgencyLearningLifecourse2007 clarify that action flows from the values and beliefs of a person. This study will try to deepen understanding on this interplay of beliefs and agency realised in the context of Agentic AI among students. As action and belief are tied together closely [@mccormickBelievingEvidence2014] it is relevant to investigate these beliefs that inform action further.

## Research Questions

How is Agentic AI changing values and beliefs of students in the ecology in which agency-as-achieved can be enacted?

#### Sub Questions

1. What values and beliefs are prevalent among students concerning Agentic AI?
2. How are prevalent beliefs disclosed in policy and teacher narratives relevant to students because of AAI?
3. In what ways are students performing academic and non-academic tasks, by either conforming or subverting rules and restrictions?

### RQ1: Thematic Analysis and UMT

### Analysis

As clarified in the Knowledge Gap, there is a close relation between action and belief, however in the context of Agentic AI the values and beliefs among students. In @kramerTeachersBeliefsComponent2019 the word _worldview_ is used to describe this belief, which in @biestaHowAgencyPossible's definition would contribute to the _ecology_. The way this is investigated in @kramerTeachersBeliefsComponent2019 is through the use of @leontievApproachingWorldviewStructure2007's Ultimate Meanings Technique (UMT). 

Where @kramerTeachersBeliefsComponent2019 used UMT to discover worldview among teachers I will investigate among a small group of students.

_Thematic analysis_ will be used as @naeemStepbyStepProcessThematic2023 and @braun2021thematic describe it to find common themes and topics in personal qualitative interview with students concerning these worldviews.

After the initial analysis and recognized larger themes questions will be formulated to be able to use a more quantitative approach in the form of a survey.

### RQ2: Critical Discourse Analyis

Through _critical discourse analyis_ (CDA) I will look at what kind of language is constructing narratives, describes relations of power and how it creates or reinforces beliefs [@blommaertCriticalDiscourseAnalysis2000]. With CDA I can take a look at school policy and try to find patterns in power dynamics and social effects in discourse. In further analysis I will analyze context and intertextuality to challenge social inequalities. I will focus mainly on step two: _Identify obstacles to addressing the social wrong_ of the CDA process as described by @fairclough2013critical. 

1. Analyse dialectical relations
2. Select texts
3. Analyse texts interdiscursively and linguistically

To assist in the Critical Discourse analysis I will use the @Cui2023 package for R to help quantify some aspects of it.

Besides investigating school policy, I will collect in-class field notes, transcripts of audio-recorded lectures and classroom talk, i.e. when students and teachers interact with each other in the classroom, and interviews with teachers.

To analyze this data I will codify the texts, look for synonyms and highlight recurring normative statements on the use of or the prevalence of AI technologies. Rereading the text can illicit patterns beyond just the words being said [@brooksRolePowerRitual2016].

### RQ3: Mixed-method

To find out where and how this impacts students lives I want to follow the academic and non-academic tasks of a small number of students to find out where AAI / GenAI is confronting students with its actions. Similar to what @ferrariUnderstandingAcademicNonacademic2000 did concerning tasks and procrastination only focusing not on task completion but on whether tasks are affected by AAI / GenAI and how students feel about this.

Students in project education will be asked to write down three tasks that they intend to complete for five consecutive days and will be asked to score along different dimensions how AAI / GenAI is affecting their completion of the task and how students deal with restrictions laid upon by school policy or assignment rules.

The analysis would then consist of comparing tasks among these dimensions, to categorize the type of tasks, their importance to the subject and to compare tasks and scoring between subjects in which way they subvert or conform to the rules.

Before doing this I would like to interview a small group of students to determine which kind of tasks and dimensions would make the most sense and what kind of AAI or GenAI tools are relevant to ask about. For the questions and categories questions from Sense of Agency-scale (SoAS) developed by @tapalsenseofagencyscale2017 will be adapted.

### Sampling and data collection

As mentioned above the initial interviews will be conducted among a group of students. To come with a representative view of students I will seek out students in different areas of expertise. Within our institute of the HAN there are students that follow programs for law, economics, teaching, medical professions, building engineering, informatics amongst others. And in different years. For the first interviews it will be difficult to distritube this evenly.

For the surveys I will go through student organizations for the different fields of expertise, which have closer relationships with students, to be able to distribute widely as well as to acquire a large number of respondents. Within the insitute there are about 30.000 students that are working on a bachelor-diploma, so it would seem feasible to come with enough respondents even if only 1% of active students respond.

For the mixed-method analysis a reward system would make sense as students would be spending quite some time on their task cards similar to the research performed by @ferrariUnderstandingAcademicNonacademic2000.
